# Criss-cross: two branches each merge the other, then get merged together - so
# git finds TWO merge bases and builds a synthetic virtual base. Base detection by
# signature can't cope with that (the shared history is re-signed on both sides);
# the content set-difference does. Both sides' changes must survive and the result
# must verify.

exec git init
exec git config user.email test@sesam.dev
exec git config user.name 'Sesam Test'

exec sesam init --user admin --install-merge
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'init sesam'

exec sesam tell --user bob --recipient $BOB_PUBKEY --group dev
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'base: bob'

# X changes bob's groups; Y adds carol. (Tags pin the pre-merge tips so we can
# build the criss-cross without capturing hashes.)
exec git checkout -b X
exec sesam user change-groups --user bob --group-add opsx
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'x1'
exec git tag x1

exec git checkout -b Y X~1
exec sesam tell --user carol --recipient $CAROL_PUBKEY --group dev
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'y1'
exec git tag y1

# X merges y1 (sesam.yml takes ours via the merge driver, config-regen is separate).
exec git checkout X
! exec git merge y1
exec git commit --no-edit

# Y merges x1 - now both branches contain a merge of the other (the criss-cross).
exec git checkout Y
! exec git merge x1
exec git commit --no-edit

# Merge Y into X: two merge bases -> synthetic virtual base. Used to fail with
# "failed to find common origin"; now resolves via the content diff.
exec git checkout X
! exec git merge Y
exec git commit --no-edit

# The doubly-merged log verifies, and both sides' changes are present.
exec sesam verify
exec sesam show .sesam/audit/log.jsonl
stdout 'opsx'
stdout '"user": "carol"'
